# MAC lookup chaos rig — takeaways

This document records what the chaos rig (`tests/chaos_rig.py`) revealed
about how `maclookup.lookup_detailed` handles messy real-world inputs.

Run the rig:

```
python3 tests/chaos_rig.py              # plain text summary
python3 tests/chaos_rig.py --md         # full Markdown report to stdout
python3 tests/chaos_rig.py --strict     # CI gate; exits 1 on any mismatch
```

The full per-case results live alongside this file in
[`chaos_report.md`](chaos_report.md) and are regenerated by
`python3 tests/chaos_rig.py --md --out tests/fixtures/chaos_report.md`.

## What the rig throws at the parser

67 cases across 13 categories, including:

* canonical formats (colon, hyphen, Cisco dotted, plain hex, space-nibble)
* CLI / OS pastes — Windows `ipconfig /all`, Linux `ifconfig` / `ip link`,
  Cisco IOS `show interfaces` + `bia`, Juniper, Arista, iDRAC / iLO
* multi-line pastes, asset-inventory CSV rows, JSON/HTML snippets,
  ticket / email prose
* wrappers and trailing punctuation (parens, brackets, quotes, backticks,
  trailing `.`, `,`, `;`, `key=value;END`)
* locally-administered / broadcast / multicast / all-zero edge cases
* longest-prefix correctness (MA-S over MA-L parent, 8-hex falling back
  to MA-L parent, 6-hex MA-L prefix only)
* partial prefixes from 4 hex up to 10 hex
* OCR-style typos (O/0, I/l, mixed with labelled inputs)
* hex-word false-positive guards (`deadbeefcafe`, `face:beef:cafe`,
  `cisco`, `3com`, `Apple Inc`)
* Unicode-fancy punctuation (en-dashes, tabs, NBSP between label and MAC)
* multi-MAC inputs (rig pins that the first plausible candidate wins)
* pathological empties and overlong runs

## Defects found & fixed

### 1. Phone-shaped tokens classified as MAC candidates (PR #13)

A token like `1-800-555-1234` has hyphens (a MAC separator) and 11
hex-valid chars (all digits are hex-valid), which is inside the 6–12
length window the extractor uses. It cleaned to `18005551234` and was
offered as a MAC candidate even though no human would read it that way.

The fix (`maclookup.py:_has_macish_grouping`) added a guard: when a
token has internal separators but contains **no hex letters (a–f)**,
its separator-delimited groups must be sized like a MAC's (2, 4, or 6),
and tokens with 4+ groups must additionally be uniformly sized.

### 2. Bare-normalize fast path bypassed the guard (PR #14)

After PR #13 shipped, the live PWA still showed `1-800-555-1234` as
*"No registry entry for prefix 180055512"*. Root cause:
`lookup_detailed` (and the JS `macLookupDetailed`) had a separate fast
path that fed `normalize_mac(input)` straight into the prefix matcher
without consulting `extract_mac_candidates`. Phone digits survived
`normalize_mac` because it only strips `[-:.\s]` — the resulting 11
all-hex chars passed the 6–12 window check and produced a `cleaned`
value with `note='partial'`, which the UI rendered as a prefix message.

The fix adds `_normalized_input_is_mac_shaped(raw)` (and JS
`normalizedInputIsMacShaped(input)`) which strips wrappers/whitespace
from the raw input and applies the same group-uniformity rule before
the fast path is allowed to surface a cleaned value. With the gate,
phone-shaped inputs end up with `cleaned=None` so the UI shows no
prefix message at all.

### 3. JS UI handler synthesized prefix from its own normalize_mac (PR #15)

After PR #14 shipped, the live PWA *still* showed *"No registry entry
for prefix 180055512"* for `1-800-555-1234`. The Python side and JS
`macLookupDetailed` were both correctly returning `cleaned=null`, but
two UI-layer functions in `web/app.js` were bypassing them:

* `isHexish(input)` was deciding whether to enter the MAC path purely
  on `stripped.length ∈ [6,12]` + hex-validity. Phone digits passed,
  so the UI routed phone queries through `macLookupDetailed`.
* `handleQuery`'s miss branch fell back to
  `(cleaned || normalizeMac(trimmed)).slice(0, 9)` when `cleaned` was
  null, which re-synthesized `180055512` from the phone and showed
  it via `tr('no_prefix', ...)`.

The fix routes phone/IP inputs to the fuzzy-vendor path instead:
`isHexish` now consults `normalizedInputIsMacShaped`, so phone shapes
return false; `handleQuery`'s miss branch only shows the prefix
message when `cleaned` is actually set, otherwise it falls through to
`fuzzyVendorSearch` (which renders an empty results state — the right
outcome for a phone number).

The three defects are covered by:

* `tests/test_chaos_rig.py::test_no_phone_numbers_become_macs`
  — asserts `extract_mac_candidates(...) == []` AND
  `lookup_detailed(...).cleaned is None` for every phone/IP probe.
* The `false-positive` category in the chaos corpus includes the bare
  phone shapes (`1-800-555-1234`, `555-1234`, `(415) 555-1212`,
  `+44-20-7946-0958`, `192.168.1.1`, `10.0.0.1`) as `expect=none`,
  pinning `cleaned=None` so any regression fails the rig.
* `tests/web/mac_formats.mjs` directly exercises
  `normalizedInputIsMacShaped`, `hasMacishGrouping`, `isHexish`, a
  simulated `macLookupDetailed`, AND a simulated `handleQuery` that
  asserts phone/IP inputs route to the fuzzy path (never producing a
  "prefix XYZ" line) while real-MAC misses still surface the prefix
  message correctly.

## Things that work today and were worth pinning

The rig also documents intentional behaviors that surprised earlier
iterations of this code and are worth not regressing:

* **En-dash separators reassemble.** `00–1A–2B–3C–4D–5E` (U+2013 dashes)
  isn't tokenized as a single run, but `_combine_whitespace_chunks`
  greedily reassembles the 2-char hex fragments back into a valid MAC.
  A friendly accident; the rig pins it as a `match`.
* **OCR I/l correction can leave the result `partial`.** When the
  corrected hex prefix isn't actually assigned in any registry we return
  `cleaned` + `partial` rather than pretending to have a vendor hit.
* **`8C:1F:64:AF` resolves to MA-L parent.** 8 hex chars is shorter than
  any MA-S/MA-M prefix, so longest-prefix falls through to the 6-char
  MA-L parent (IEEE Registration Authority). Confirms the longest-prefix
  fallback chain is wired correctly.
* **All-zero MAC resolves to Xerox.** `00:00:00:00:00:00` matches the
  Xerox MA-L assignment (`000000`). Surprising-but-correct.
* **Hex blobs outside the 6–12 char window are rejected outright.** A
  64-char hash, a 100-char run of "00", or a 13-char hex string with no
  separators all return `none` rather than silently picking the first
  six chars and pretending to have found a MAC.
* **Inputs shorter than 6 hex chars never produce a `cleaned` value.**
  `00:1A:2` (5 hex) and `00:1A` (4 hex) both return `none` — below the
  candidate floor.
* **Wrappers and trailing punctuation are universally stripped.** Every
  combination tested (`()`, `[]`, `<>`, `{}`, `''`, `""`, backticks,
  trailing `.,;`, `key=value;END`) resolves correctly.
* **Multi-MAC pastes don't collapse.** `00:1A:7D:AA:BB:CC` on one line
  and `00:00:00:11:22:33` on the next stay separate; both appear in
  `extract_mac_candidates`.

## How the rig is used by CI

* `tests/test_chaos_rig.py` is picked up by the existing
  `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` step in
  `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. Any future regression in messy-input
  handling fails CI with a per-case message.
* The Markdown snapshot in `tests/fixtures/chaos_report.md` is
  committed so a reviewer can see the corpus and the actual behavior
  side by side in a PR diff without having to run the rig locally.
